newsitem.title: USA: U.S. budget deficit narrows slightly in February.
newsitem.headline: U.S. budget deficit narrows slightly in February.

text.p: The government's spending deficit narrowed slightly to $44.01 billion in February from a year earlier as a strong economy generated healthy revenues, the Treasury Department said Friday.
The monthly shortfall between spending and income was 0.8 percent lower in February this year than in February 1996 when it was $44.35 billion.

February's deficit followed a $13.36 billion surplus in January -- typically a surplus month as year-end revenues from corporations and payments from individuals who pay their taxes on a quarterly basis flow into the government's coffers.
Total revenues from taxes as well as from fees and other sources rose to $90.29 billion in February from $89.43 billion a year earlier. In January this year, revenues were $150.72 billion.
Spending on all types of government programmes in February totalled $134.30 billion, down from $137.35 billion in January but up from $133.78 billion in February 1996.

During the first five months of fiscal 1997 that ends on Sept. 30, the cumulative budget deficit was up 11.6 percent to $89.96 billion from $80.64 billion in the comparable first five months of fiscal 1996.
The Clinton administration is forecasting that the deficit for the full 1997 fiscal year will rise to $125.59 billion from a shortfall of $106.99 billion in fiscal 1996.

Congress and the White House are trying to get talks going about the administration's proposed fiscal 1998 budget. The congressional side is led by Senate Budget Comittee Chairman Pete Domenici, a New Mexico Republican who has threatened to bring up his own budget plan with steep spending cuts and no tax cut unless negotiations start soon.

Republicans say President Bill Clinton's budget proposal is flawed and would result in a $69 billion deficit in 2002, the year the president said it would balance. They have also protested Clinton's "unwillingness" to address the consumer price index issue as an obstacle to serious budget negotiations.
